subsections.heading: Houthi-claimed strikes on two Saudi airports

paragraphs.text: Three civilians were killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia. The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others. The attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents. Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile.

The Gulf Cooperation Council secretary-general, Jassim Mohammed al-Budaiwi, described the attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports as "systematic crimes" targeting civilians. He said that "endangering the lives of travellers, workers and civilians" is "a dangerous escalation and a flagrant violation of international laws and norms".

The Saudi-led coalition said it struck 82 Houthi military targets in Yemen in what it called a "comprehensive operation". Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement posted on X that the targets included "11 mountain-based ballistic missile storage sites in Saada", along with "command and control centres, communications systems, missile and weapons depots, and a gathering site", across Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib. The claim is the coalition own account and is not independently confirmed in the report.

A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles in an incident 51 nautical miles north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Wednesday, with casualties reported. The agency issued the incident as UKMTO Warning 158-26. No exact number of projectiles or casualties was given, and no party was identified as responsible.

sections.heading: US Military Posture and the Election Calendar

subsections.heading: Preparations to resume major combat operations

paragraphs.text: The Pentagon instructed US Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, according to US officials. If major combat operations resume, they are expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets. The directive did not include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump has not made any final decisions. A Pentagon official said: "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President."

The report states it could happen before the US midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier, citing a source who said "The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out" and that "After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly". A White House official said "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States". A second Israeli official said "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased".

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, referred to "Our considerations and conditions for ending the imposed war on all fronts" and said "The necessary response to the other side's proposals will also be delivered through mediators".

On the other side of the same channel, Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian reply to a US counterproposal that included nuclear concessions. Israeli officials characterised the Iranian leadership as "desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first".

No casualty figure for civilians killed or injured by US or Israeli strikes inside Iran could be sourced for this reporting window. The only in-window report of activity at a struck Iranian site concerns the Pentagon directive naming Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets as expected objectives if major combat operations resume; it carries no casualty count.

subsections.heading: Civilians harmed by the Iranian state

paragraphs.text: Alireza Sepahi, 25, and Alireza Raissi, 21, were hanged on the morning of 5 October at Isfahan's central prison. According to the judiciary's Mizan agency they were convicted of membership of an armed group and endangering national security, in a case concerning protests in Isfahan's Alikhani Square on 8 January in which authorities say four police officers were killed. Sepahi had been spared a public execution in July after a heart attack, and the night before his execution he married Mahshad Kashani, 22, in a telephone ceremony conducted by their lawyer.

Iran Human Rights, a Norway-based organisation, reported that Iran has executed 34 people over the protests, which peaked on 8 and 9 January. The US-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center said the case had "serious procedural flaws", including disregard for defence evidence, and its co-founder Roya Boroumand said the marriage took place "in absentia". Mai Sato, the UN special rapporteur on human rights in Iran, said that for Sepahi's family "the horror continued" after the execution, as his body was taken to Kashan rather than returned for burial in Isfahan. Rights groups say the protests were crushed in a crackdown that killed thousands, accompanied by an internet blackout.
